content.thinking:
I'm thinking through the koala's design - roughly real-world size at about 70cm, clinging vertically to a eucalyptus branch mounted on a stand, hugging the trunk-like form.

I'm weighing different poses — maybe the koala sits at a branch fork facing the viewer with arms gripping a horizontal branch in front, or alternatively hugs a vertical trunk facing it directly. I'll settle on a vertical trunk at the origin with the koala's front oriented toward it, arms wrapping around to grip the back side.

Let me settle on a clearer composition: a base log plinth with a trunk rising and forking, with the koala sitting upright in the fork. Actually a simpler pose works better: the koala perches on a horizontal branch running along the X axis like a bird on a perch, supported by a trunk forking off to one side.

I'll build a log-slab base with a thick vertical trunk, a horizontal perch branch with a diagonal brace, and a leafy shoot at the far end. The koala sits at the branch's center, one arm raising a leafy twig toward its mouth while the other grips the perch, legs angled forward with feet wrapping the branch to sit naturally.

I'll just commit to a horizontal perch branch with the koala seated on top, rump resting on the branch and legs bent with feet gripping in front, and start pinning down exact coordinates for the branch and hips.

I'm working out the shoot geometry — deciding it should rise diagonally from the perch so one hand can hold it naturally, and double-checking the arm lengths fit the koala's body proportions so the grip looks right.

Now I'm sorting out koala body proportions: rump near the branch top around 0.44, head and ears peaking near 1.0, giving a seated height of roughly 0.6 m, with the overall scene bounds landing near 1.35 m tall and about 1 m wide including the stand. I'm also weighing whether to build the rounded body from simple boxes or something smoother, since koalas are much more rounded than boxy shapes would suggest.

For style I'm leaning toward blending smooth low-poly sweeps with chunky pixel-style cell painting for the body, keeping facet counts low (6-8 sides) to preserve a blocky silhouette, while the head gets a wide sphere-based shape with fluffy stepped-disc ears and a painted pixel-art face decal for the nose and features.

Still orienting ear discs outward with fluff cards, then thinking about adding small textured fur tuft cards across the body using pixel-art alpha quads.

Now I'm planning the skeleton: root at hips, with a spine chain running from hips up to chest with a slight forward lean.

Setting the perch branch position, then placing the koala's hip joint and building out a pear-shaped body with increasing radii from rump to belly to chest to neck. I'm chaining the spine joints upward to a neck base and head center, checking that the overall sitting height stays proportional to real koala dimensions.

Scaling it down into a chibi-style proportion: a head radius around 0.12 with wide cheeks, ears sticking up near the top, and a spine chain from hips through two spine joints to the neck and head center, aiming the head slightly forward and up.

I'll settle on hips as the root joint, then build the spine chain starting from that same position outward through three spans, naming them spine1, spine2, spine3 with role spine.

For the neck and head, I'll create a two-span chain from P3 up to the head base, naming segments neck1 and neck2, then attach a separate head joint at the tip facing forward-up with a small jaw piece underneath for the koala's short muzzle. Since koalas don't have tails, I'll skip that chain entirely.

For the hind legs, I'm working through the sitting pose geometry -- hips positioned outward, thighs angling forward, and figuring out where the knees, shins, and feet land relative to the branch so the feet can wrap around and grip it from below rather than colliding with the thigh or branch itself.

I'm thinking the toes could curl around the branch as small arcing capsule chains, maybe two joints each per toe, to keep the joint count manageable within the limit.

Now I'm placing the shoulders symmetrically and working out the left arm's shoulder-elbow-wrist-hand chain so it reaches down to grip the perch branch, though I notice the hand position might overlap with where the foot already sits on the branch.

The right arm reaches up to grasp a leafy eucalyptus shoot near the mouth, with the stem curving from the perch upward through a few bends before fanning into leaves at the top, plus another shoot positioned behind for fullness.

I'm planning to define the stem as a curve and derive the hand's grip position directly from a point along that curve, offset slightly toward the body, so the wrist naturally wraps around the branch rather than being placed arbitrarily.

Now I'm designing the stand itself: a vertical eucalyptus trunk off to one side with a fork, a horizontal perch branch extending from it with leafy tips, a diagonal brace for support, and a flat plinth base at the bottom to anchor the whole structure.

I'll make the slab a round wood slice with bark rim, a thick leaning trunk growing from one side up to leaves with a perch branch, and a shorter stump on the opposite side topped with a leafy sprig to balance it. For eucalyptus foliage, I'm planning drooping crescent-shaped leaves in muted blue-green and grey tones, using light/dark pixel leaf textures clustered on a few twigs for a natural look.

I'm also adding bumnuts and peeling bark strips to the trunk, then working out texel density so the body paint resolution stays sharp relative to the model's scale -- roughly 0.02 cell size giving good texel coverage on a 1024 paint sheet. Keeping part count low with one card per texture, sides at 8 for smooth sweeps, and now setting up a koala grey-to-light fur ramp with a cream belly palette.

Rather than blending the belly color smoothly, I want a dithered cell-based boundary so the cream patch reads as fur texture rather than a gradient -- using forward-facing normals and vertical position to define the chest/belly region with noise-based shading for the torso base tone.

Now I'm nailing down koala-specific features: grey body fur, fluffy round ears with white tufts, a large black leathery nose, small dark eyes, white chin and cheeks, white chest fluff, and a white rump with brownish spots like real koalas. For the hands I want the distinctive two-opposable-thumb anatomy -- five digits split as two on one side opposing three, with pale claws.

Now I'm structuring the head geometry region by region.

Building the head from a scaled sphere, with separate cheek spheres and a small boxy muzzle. For the nose I'm shaping a big elongated black oval that protrudes across the top of the muzzle, using a flattened scaled sphere with a tiny light highlight pixel on top. For the eyes I'm placing small black bead spheres with tiny white highlight boxes, positioned onto the head surface.

For the mouth, I'm adding a decal line across the muzzle underside and a small separate cream-colored lower jaw part positioned at the jaw joint, with a dark interior patch tucked behind to suggest a closed mouth gap.

Now I'm working on fluffy cheek and chin texture using scattered fur cards, and figuring out how to place white tuft cards along the ear rims specifically rather than across the whole ear surface, filtering scatter hits by their normal direction so fluff only appears on the rim edges.

I'm designing the ear shape as a stepped pixel outline using column spans to approximate a rounded contour, then layering a smaller cream inner-ear shape on top with slightly greater thickness, and tilting the whole ear outward about 25 degrees.

For the skeleton, I'm planning single hinge joints for each ear attached at the head, and separate arm chains running from shoulder to elbow to wrist (parented to the chest spine) that will be skinned with a smooth sweep along the joint path for the limb mesh.

For hands and feet, I'm sketching a helper that builds each digit as a short two-segment chain, giving roughly 20 finger joints and 20 toe joints alongside the spine, neck, head, jaw, ear, and hip joints for about 60 joints total. I'm also working out how the gripping hand should wrap its digits in a circular arc around the branch axis so the fingers curl naturally around it.

Computing the finger arc positions using angle θ from top (0°) to front (90°), with fingers starting around 40° and curling to 170° under the branch, spaced along the axis; thumbs mirror from the opposite side wrapping back over for an opposed grip.

For the hand gripping the stem, I'm deriving perpendicular basis vectors from the tangent direction using cross products rather than lookAt, since the SDK restricts that. For the feet, I'm wrapping toes around the perch from front (70°) to underneath (200°), spacing them along the axis, with the hallux opposed from the other side — placing the ankle anchor point relative to the branch center.

Now I'm computing the actual ankle coordinates along the branch circumference, then checking shin and thigh segment lengths from knee to ankle and hip to knee to make sure the proportions are plausible (~0.19 and ~0.22 units). I'm also checking how the rump sits relative to the branch — since the branch passes near the hip region, I need to verify the rump's radius doesn't awkwardly intersect the branch geometry.

Realizing the branch is buried inside the rump with the current placement, I'm repositioning the hips further back and up so the rump actually rests on top of the branch like a koala sitting in a fork, recalculating the branch center and rump offsets to avoid overlap.

I'm plotting the spine as a curve from the hips up through the shoulders to the head, estimating the head position and resulting total height — but the seated height comes out taller than a real koala, so I'm considering shortening the torso to keep the proportions stubbier and more chibi-like.

Still defining the torso sweep shape...

Now positioning the hip and thigh roots, tapering thigh radii, and placing the shoulders symmetrically to match the chest radius at that point along the chain.

I'm tracing the left arm's joint chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist, landing the wrist on the perch's surface using a wrap offset, then verifying segment lengths stay consistent. For the right arm, I'm starting to define a stem point it will hold.

Now I'm plotting the stem as a curve rising from the perch root up toward the mouth area, trying candidate control points so the stem reads naturally and estimating where the right hand grips it along the way.

For the arm, I'm positioning shoulder, elbow, and wrist so the hand lands on the grip point, computing the wrist as a small offset from that grip position toward the body. I'm also confirming the stem's leaves sit along the upper portion without colliding with the face, and noting the head faces forward toward the viewer while the stem stays to the left side.

Now I'm designing the base layout: a wooden plinth with planked texture and a moss patch, then building a curved trunk using a catmull spline that tapers from thicker at the base to thinner near a fork, where a perch branch extends outward to meet it.

Mapping out the shoot path curving up from the stump toward the koala's hand position.

Checking the elbow-wrist bone lengths for the right arm, they come out close enough to the left arm's proportions. I also want to make sure the stem tip doesn't collide with the mouth area, so I'm comparing its z-position against the head's muzzle projection.

I'm adding a second branch from trunk A arching over the koala's head with hanging leaf clusters for visual balance against the smaller stump B, and setting overall scene bounds for x and y. I'm also planning the bark paint details using layered grey-green tones.

Still working on texture details...

I'm skipping the plaque idea and instead scattering flat leaf cards, low pebble shapes, a tiny mushroom, and grass tufts on the plinth. For the koala, I'm adding cream claw cones on the digit tips, ear and cheek fur cards, nose and eye details, brown rump spots, cream chest fur, and maybe a small leaf card poking from its mouth for a cute touch.

Now I'm designing the pixel leaf texture itself—crescent-shaped, tapering with a lighter midrib, built procedurally by varying width per row and blending green and blue-grey tones so the leaf can hang naturally from the koala's mouth or sit among the scattered foliage cards.

Next I'm setting up card frames along the stem sweeps, placing leaves at angled offsets (around ±70 and 160 degrees) so they fan outward from the branch, with lean toward the downward flow direction and double-sided cards so orientation doesn't matter visually.

For fur, I'm sketching a small pixel-art tuft pattern, narrow at top and broad at the base like a tapering spike, using white and light-gray shades that will tint based on the paint color read at the root so the fur matches each part's resolved color.

I'm sizing fur cards small and leaning them at a steep angle so they flow downward across roughly 300 instances, keeping the tint blending into the cream chest region and torso color. For the eyes, I'm designing a tiny 4x4 pixel decal with a dark iris and single highlight pixel to give a shiny koala-eye look.

For the nose, I'm using a color ramp with a highlighted gray patch toward the top to simulate a soft sheen, and building the muzzle as a scaled sphere protruding from the lower face with the nose set at its tip. I'm adding a dark slab for the inner mouth line and a cream chin below, then placing cheek tufts by scattering cards on the head surface filtered to the side-and-lower regions to mimic koala cheek fluff.

Now I'm figuring out ear placement and orientation, working out world coordinates for the head and ear joints and how the head bone should aim slightly upward and forward so the ears sit naturally on the sides.

I'm placing the jaw joint beneath the head, hinged near the back of the mouth, and figuring out where the lower jaw box sits relative to the skull. Then I'm computing the eye socket positions as offsets from the head sphere's center, accounting for its scaled width, height, and depth.

Now I'm sizing the nose and sketching a stylized koala face proportion—small wide-set eyes, an oversized central nose—before moving into writing the fur color palette constants.

Still writing shaders...

Still writing shading logic...

I should keep the flat color palette modest, under the limit, and now I'm sketching a helper function that generates points swept around a circular cross-section given a center, axis, and radius, using a basis derived from the axis and an up vector.

For the stem, the axis is the tangent direction at the grip, and I need to pick an up vector and compute the perpendicular basis the same way. I'm figuring out where the hand grips the stem—computing the angle θ0 toward the wrist position so I can decide which direction the fingers and thumb wrap from, choosing the wrap direction so it goes across the side facing the viewer.

Now I'm sketching a generic gripper function that takes a side, wrist joint, center, axis, radius, and wrap sign, then builds each digit as a short chain of two joints with tapering radius and rounded caps, adding a small claw spike at the tip oriented along the last bone's direction. I'm working out where each digit's base point sits relative to the palm center using the wrap angle.

The palm sphere sits at the wrist bone, parenting digits to the arm chain's tip joint. I need to mirror this for feet, with an ankle tip joint, sole palm sphere, and four toes plus a hallux wrapping around the perch's front-lower curve starting near θ0 = 55°.

Working out the angular placement for feet and hands around the perch cylinder: feet ankle starts around 60°, toes sweep forward to about 170°, and the hallux curls back toward -20° to avoid the rump. Hands follow similar logic with fingers sweeping to 150° and thumbs curling back near -10°, with small offsets along the perch axis for finger spacing.

I'll skip adding a tail stub, and decide the torso gets its own paint treatment while limbs are grey with darker leathery paws and hands.

Writing paw and face color logic...

Now moving to the stand: I'm building a plinth using a tiled box with wood-plank texturing, setting up the UV mapping so planks run along the x-axis at pixel resolution.

I'm layering the plinth with a lower wider wood slab and an upper slightly narrower earth/moss-topped slab, giving it a stepped, sunken appearance into the floor rather than adding separate corner feet.

Now I'm planning the main trunk as a curved catmull path rising from the plinth with tapering radius and bark texture, plus a few root spikes flaring out at the base, and I'm sketching the first perch branch curving outward from partway up the trunk.

Still adding scene elements...

Still plotting branch sweeps...

Adding bend to curl leaf tips toward the flow direction for extra droop, and estimating total leaf card count across the branches. Now I'm sketching two pixel leaf textures with a tapered crescent shape for width and curvature variation.

Adding a yellowish-green leaf variant, then moving to small gumnut spheres with caps along the branch, and sketching bark grain texture using stretched noise sampling for streak patterns.

I'm deciding flat colors suffice for the remaining parts, no special naming needed, and settling on a neutral clinging pose as acceptable rest position for the eye decals and brow shading. Now I'm working out the sweep API for the torso, using a chain-based spine path so the body skin bends naturally across the hip-to-shoulder range.

I'm defining interpolated radii along the torso profile—wider at hips and belly, narrowing at the chest and neck base—using a linear interpolation helper between keyframe points. Then I'm checking that the rounded bottom cap sphere nestles cleanly against the leg branch without gaps, nudging the hip joint position slightly to close a small overlap.

That gives distance 0.2154 against the sum 0.211, so a tiny gap of 0.004 — close enough to count as touching. I'll build the spine chain upward from there with P1, P2, P3, and place the hip joint at P0 with thighs symmetric at ±0.13, then work out the knee position and check its clearance against the branch.

Continuing down the leg, I compute the ankle position from the knee using the shin's angle and verify the shin segment length is reasonable with a tapering radius. Looking at the x-positions, the legs and the hand gripping the stem stay well separated, so no collision there — but checking the arm, I find the left elbow position nearly coincides with the knee location, which is a real overlap I need to fix.

Estimating the right wrist position from the grip point on the stem, then checking shoulder-to-elbow and elbow-to-wrist lengths for plausibility, and confirming the stem's path clears the head given its width.

Setting head and ear coordinates, then planning the chain structure: arm chains with shoulder/elbow/wrist joints, digit chains for fingers, and role assignments like "leg", "arm", "spine", "neck", "head", "jaw", and "hinge" for ears, plus how to parent the head joint to the neck chain's tip.

I'm now working out the neck as its own short chain with two spans connecting into the head sphere, deciding whether to keep the torso sweep separate from the neck sweep so the radius tapers correctly under the head.

For the head itself, I'm building a skull sphere with low poly count and non-uniform scaling to get the right skull shape, keeping the facets since the paint is cell-snapped anyway, then placing the eye decal on that skull surface.

Now I'm working out eye decal placement by computing where the skull surface sits at a given x,y so the eyes sit right on the front curve, mirroring for the right side. Then I'm sizing and positioning a muzzle sphere that protrudes less than a typical animal muzzle, fitting a koala's flatter face, with the nose sitting just in front of it.

I continue placing the nose, jaw sphere, and dark mouth interior slab, adding cheek tuft spheres with fur cards, and noting the head and ear parts get their own color and bone assignments.

Now I'm setting up the ear joints angled outward and upward from the head, then working out the extrusion grid for the ear shape, centering the stepped outline so it aligns properly on each side.

Working out ear orientation vectors...

Working out the local axis vectors so the ear's x-axis and normal stay consistent for both left and right sides, then using that normal to offset the inner ear detail slightly forward for the extrude.

Now I'm scattering fluff cards along the ear rim, filtering hits where the normal is roughly tangent to the rim direction, using a cream tint and upward flow for the lean. I'm also adding grey fur to the ear backs, then setting up torso fur cards with a denser scatter, filtered to avoid the belly, with longer cards leaning back and down to follow the torso's fur direction, picking up color from the underlying paint.

Extending this to the thighs, arms, and head, with skull-area fur filtered away from the face. For the paws I'm defining a dark ramp of paint colors for the pads, pale spikes for the claws, and sticking fur cards onto hit points so they inherit bone transforms. For the plinth decorations I'm shaping small rotated pebble boxes and a tiny pixel-style mushroom using a cylinder stem and a partial hemisphere cap textured with red-and-white spot pixel art.

I'm scattering grass tuft cards around the base using upward-facing frames, adding flattened fallen leaf cards on the plinth, and covering the top with a moss-and-dirt tile texture plus wood plank sides. I'm checking the builder's type signatures for cards, parts, and frames before writing the TypeScript imports and starting the actual component code.

Writing import statements...

Now I'm defining color ramps — grey and cream palettes snapped to 64 color levels, plus a texel constant and helper functions for profiling shapes and quantizing colors.

Writing fur painting logic...

Writing fur speckle and limb shading logic...

For the ear, I'm shading the outer ramp lighter grey while painting the inner ear cream with a subtle pink hint near the center, using the distance from the center point to drive that blend.

Now I'm writing the bark painting function, sampling noise at different frequencies to decide between a rust color variant and a base gum color blend...

Writing more color ramps...

I need to design a wood plank texture tile for the plinth, sizing texels so the pixel density scales correctly whether the face is small or large relative to the tile.

For the side face, the crop fits within the tile without magnification, but the top face needs a larger texel scale since it's bigger than the tile, which is fine since it'll mostly be covered by the moss slab anyway. I'll randomize crop positions using a seeded rng for variety, then move on to designing the moss tile with dithered green, dirt patches, and tiny flowers for the top slab.

Now I'm working out the plinth's layering: setting a lower tier at height 0.07 and an upper tier at 0.05 stacked on top, with trunks starting around y=0.1 to sit flush on the upper plinth surface. I'm skipping extra plaque decoration to keep things simple, then starting to write out the leaf texture generator function that builds a pixel texture using rib, midtone, edge, and dark colors.

Writing leaf texture pixels...

Then I'm defining how to scatter leaf cards onto the frames using three leaf variants with size, lean, flow direction, bend, and spin parameters to create natural-looking foliage clusters.

I'm sizing leaf texels relative to the main body texel to keep detail consistent, then planning a helper function that builds twig sweep frames by sampling positions and angles along stems, accumulating them into a shared leaf frame array before issuing a single batched draw call per distinct leaf texture.

Now I'm adding small gumnut spheres with tiny cylinder caps scattered along the stem, bark flaps on the trunk, root spikes radiating from the trunk base, and a textured disc for the stump top using concentric pixel rings mapped onto the cylinder's cap UV.

For other scene elements, I'm planning flat leaf cards for the floor lying horizontal, grass blades built from a pixel-art texture arranged in crossed cards near the plinth top, and small flat pebble boxes rotated slightly and colored in muted greys.

Thinking about decoration, I'll skip text on the plinth and instead add a tiny pixel-art leaf emblem decal on its front face as a plane, then move on to fur texture cards using a tufted pixel sprite that can be tinted per-instance.

I'm writing a wrap helper that positions points evenly around a cylindrical axis (like wrapping feathers or decorations around a perch), computing orthogonal basis vectors from the axis and a reference direction, then placing each point by angle and radius along that axis.

Now I'm figuring out the hand/wrist setup, computing the wrist position by wrapping a point around the arm's axis at a given angle and radius, so the arm chain can connect properly to the hand.

For the fingers and thumbs, I'm spacing them along the branch axis with small offsets so they don't overlap, using opposite wrap angles for thumbs versus fingers to keep them positioned correctly relative to the wrist.

Still planning the digit geometry... I'm laying out each digit with four points across its length giving three phalange segments, naming them systematically, and adding tapering sweep radii, rounded caps, and a tiny claw spike at the fingertip along the tangent direction.

For the thumb I'm mirroring the direction sign and using similar angle offsets at the joints. For the feet, I'm accounting for koala anatomy—fusing two toes together, giving the hallux no claw—and setting up angle offsets for the wrapped toe placement around the ankle point, using world-up as the reference axis for the foot's orientation.

For the hand gripping the stem, I'm computing the wrist position and direction along the branch tangent, then determining the wrap direction by checking which side faces the viewer so the fingers curl naturally over the front of the perch, applying the same logic symmetrically for both hands.

Now I'm defining tapering arm thickness along each limb segment for a muscular koala build, making sure the perch arm clears the knee, then adding brow tufts and scattered surface detail cards across the arms and skull.

I'm planning the mouth leaf placement near the snout, aiming for a part count around 150-200 by layering grouped cards, plus fine details like claws and tiny nostril highlight pixels on the nose.

Checking that decal targets, card colors, and part geometry typing all line up, then moving on to writing the file with proper leaf frame counts and fur flow settings.

input.command: ls; ls samples | head; grep -n "texture" src/builder.ts | head -20; grep -n "scale" src/builder.ts | head -20
